part_title: Textract, Enterprise Search and Human Review
review_basis: Visually inspected all 29 original public/course-visuals/aif-course/module-08 numbered WebP images individually in order. Narration rewritten following exact diagram arrows, visible text/examples, numeric values, callouts, and exam comparisons, with product lifecycle caveats.

scenes.title: Amazon Textract
scenes.narration: The top row is a scanned invoice PDF moving into Amazon Textract AnalyzeDocument. The output is split into text, form key-value fields and tables. The next large panel shows how application code can normalize those extracted fields into a structured JSON-like record. The example contains invoice number INV-100, vendor Example Co, date 2024-01-15 and two line items: two units of Product A at 10 dollars and one Service B at 22 dollars, yielding a 42 dollar total. The bottom left reproduces the sample invoice, and the middle panel shows partial detected text, the line-item table, key-value fields and application-normalized data. Textract returns blocks and relationships; the normalized business record is assembled by downstream application code. The right exam panel says Comprehend analyzes language meaning while Textract extracts document structure. Neither extracting an invoice nor summarizing it authorizes a payment; validate totals and fields before using them.

scenes.title: Amazon Kendra
scenes.narration: The upper left shows company documents in Amazon S3 and SharePoint. Arrows lead to Amazon Kendra connectors and a search index that make enterprise material searchable. The employee then asks, Where is IT support? The result panel highlights See the IT support page and an IT Support FAQ source, with a second laptop setup guide ranked lower. Below the flow, a feedback loop carries relevant or not relevant ratings back toward relevance tuning. This is a ranked-search experience, not a chatbot inventing a new policy. The lower worked example repeats the exact query and first result. The right-hand comparison explains that Kendra returns passages and links while Amazon Q Business historically offered a conversational assistant composed from authorized company sources. Both names appear for exam recognition, but Kendra is closed to new customers and Q Business also has lifecycle restrictions. For a new project, review supported Bedrock Knowledge Base or Amazon Quick approaches.

scenes.title: Amazon Mechanical Turk
scenes.narration: Start with the three unlabeled product photos at the upper left: a mug, a shoe and a backpack. The machine learning team submits small Human Intelligence Tasks, or H I T s, through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Human workers assign the labels mug, shoe and backpack. The requester then reviews completed tasks and accepts suitable results. Only then is a labeled dataset ready for training or another machine-learning workflow. The lower illustration repeats the same images before and after human labeling. The right-hand exam notes emphasize that Mechanical Turk is a human task marketplace, not an AI model that predicts the labels automatically. Amazon A2I may historically connect human reviewers to model outputs, but that is a distinct workflow. A good labeling task defines unambiguous categories, checks disagreements and protects private data from inappropriate public workforce exposure.

scenes.title: Human labeling workflow
scenes.narration: Follow the six numbered boxes in the main diagram. First, unlabeled photos of packages are stored in Amazon S3. Second, a labeling task is defined with categories such as intact package and damaged package; the slide illustrates Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth as the orchestration tool. Third, choose an eligible private, vendor or public labeling workforce. Fourth, compare worker responses and resolve disagreements through quality checks. Fifth, write the curated labeled images back to S3. Sixth, use those examples to train a machine-learning model. The lower worked example visibly contrasts an intact shipping box with a damaged box, tracks the same labeling steps, and ends with a model trained to detect damaged packages. The lower-right notes distinguish labels used to train a model from A2I human review of inference results. Both Ground Truth and A2I are legacy offerings closed to new customers according to the course notes; the general quality-control pattern remains important.

scenes.title: Amazon Augmented AI (A2I)
scenes.narration: Read the top process as a branching architecture. An invoice enters Amazon Textract, which predicts fields such as the total. The confidence and policy check then splits the path. High-confidence fields allowed by policy proceed to the client automatically along the green line. Low-confidence or policy-selected fields follow the amber line to Amazon A2I human review, where a reviewer verifies or corrects the field before the client receives it. A dotted optional path can add reviewed data to an S3 training dataset, but retraining is not automatic. The worked invoice example below shows an uncertain total written as 100 with a question mark; after review the verified result is 100 dollars and zero cents. The exam multiple-choice box correctly prefers selective review over sending every prediction for manual processing. There is no universal confidence threshold. A2I represents an existing-customer pattern, not a guaranteed new service onboarding path.
